newsitem.title: USA: Hurricane Danny rakes southern Alabama.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Danny rakes southern Alabama.

text.p: Torrential rains and high winds from Hurricane Danny flooded roads, downed trees and snapped power lines along the Alabama coast on Saturday, as the storm clung stubbornly to the warm waters of Mobile Bay.

After drifting out of the Gulf of Mexico in the predawn hours, Danny stalled about 35 miles southeast of the city of Mobile and remained nearly stationary with sustained winds of 80 mph into the afternoon.
The National Weather Service, which had expected landfall early Saturday, issued a new advisory saying the hurricane could be offshore until as late as Sunday.
"It's dumped a tremendous amount of rain on us," Baldwin County Emergency Management spokeswoman Leigh Anne Ryals said.
Downpours of nearly 30 inches were recorded unofficially in some areas by Doppler radar as flash floods smothered roads and low-lying areas with knee-deep currents.
"It's miserable," complained Bill McIntosh, a resident of Fort Morgan, Alabama, who said as much as four feet of water had swamped roadways near his home.
"It's a lot worse than we expected. We're having a rough time of it," he said.
Power lines collapsed under fallen trees across the area, cutting off power to an estimated 19,000 residents in coastal Mobile and Baldwin counties.

At midday, authorities closed a north-south bridge along state highway 59 which connected the mainland southeast of Mobile with the barrier island resort towns of Gulf Shores, Palmetto Beach and Fort Morgan.

Hurricane warnings remained in effect from Gulfport, Mississippi, to Apalachicola, Florida, while forecasters issued tornado watches for southeastern Mississippi, southern Alabama, the western Florida Panhandle and southwestern Georgia.
Still a minimal hurricane, Danny was expected to be downgraded quickly to tropical-storm status once it moved inland. But the hurricane defied forecasters by remaining over water.
"This is a very unusual situation," said Bill Williams, a private meteorologist in Mobile. "These types of storms usually move on through. But I expect this one to take all day. It's bizarre."
Winds downed 50 to 100 oak trees on the picturesque grounds of the antebellum Grand Hotel Resort in Point Clear, Alabama, which juts out from the eastern shore of Mobile Bay.
"We lost at least one oak estimated to be 250 years old," said Reed Pullan, who manages the 550-acre resort community. A wedding was expected to proceed as planned at the hotel later in the day.

In Gulf Shores, winds downed a four-storey condominium that was under construction and tore the roof off a nearby restaurant. Eyewitnesses said waves were breaking over the town's seawall as the storm flung debris into the streets.
Danny briefly came ashore Friday in Louisiana, between Grand Isle and the mouth of the Mississippi River, before moving back into the Gulf on a lumbering northeasterly track.

Police initially attributed two deaths to the hurricane's approach on Friday. But emergency management officials later said the heart attack of an elderly man who was securing his boat in Pirate's Cove, Alabama, was not storm-related.
Near Fort Morgan, a local beach patrol discovered the only storm fatality -- a man who died in his swamped sailboat that had broken up in heavy waves.
A state of emergency remained in effect for southern Alabama. But officials said inland shelters were hardly filled.
About 1,500 people took up temporary residence in 16 Red Cross shelters open in Alabama.
"It's fewer than last year when a big storm came through," said Red Cross spokeswoman Rene Quaresma in Point Clear.
"There comes a time when people have evacuated before and the storm has missed them. But it's important that they get to a shelter, especially if they live in low-lying areas."
